Every bridge has one job: to carry a load from one bank to the other without falling down.
A plank across a stream is the simplest kind, and it bends a little as you walk across it.
The top of the plank is squeezed, and the bottom is stretched.
An arch turns that problem around, so every stone is pushed against its neighbors.
Stone is strong when it's squeezed, which is why Roman arches are still standing.
A suspension bridge hangs its road from cables, and the cables pull on towers at each end.
So the real question is never just how strong a bridge is, but where its forces go.
Once you can see that, every bridge you drive across starts to look a little different.
Bread starts as four plain things: flour, water, salt and yeast.
Yeast is alive, and when it's warm and fed, it breathes out tiny bubbles of gas.
Kneading the dough builds a stretchy web called gluten, which traps those bubbles.
Leave it in a warm spot for an hour, and the dough slowly doubles in size.
In the oven, the bubbles swell one last time before the crust sets around them.
That's why a good loaf is full of holes, and why a cold kitchen makes a heavy one.
Too much salt slows the yeast down, and too little lets it run wild.
Bakers have been balancing those few things for thousands of years.
Next time you slice a loaf, look closely at the holes; each one is a tiny breath.

On that map, Greenland looks about as big as Africa.
In fact, Africa is roughly fourteen times larger.
Other maps keep areas true instead, and their shapes look oddly stretched.

People often ask why the sky is blue.
The short answer is that sunlight is a mix of every color, and the air scatters some colors more than others.
Blue light has a short wavelength, so it bounces around the sky much more than red light does.
Wherever you look, some of that scattered blue is heading toward your eyes.
So why are sunsets orange?
When the sun is low, its light crosses far more air to reach you.
By then, most of the blue has been scattered away, and the reds and oranges are what's left.
It's the same sunlight, just taking a longer road.
All summer long, a leaf is green because it's full of chlorophyll.
Chlorophyll catches sunlight and turns it into food for the tree.
When the days get shorter, the tree stops making it.
As the green fades, the yellows and oranges that were there all along start to show.
Some trees also make new red colors in the autumn, which is why maples look like they're on fire.
A few weeks later, the leaves fall, and the tree rests until spring.
Look inside an ordinary door lock, and you'll find a row of tiny pins.
Each pin is split into two pieces, and they come in different lengths.
Springs push the pins down, so they block the cylinder from turning.
When the right key slides in, its ridges lift every pin to exactly the right height.
The splits line up along the edge of the cylinder, and it's free to turn.
The wrong key lifts some pins too far and others not far enough.
That's the whole trick: a handful of pins, and one key that fits them all.
